steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar Backbone  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (lacks an oxygen atom on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  

3. Strand Structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.  

4. Location in the Cell  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (in eukaryotes) and in organelles (mitochondria, chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is found throughout the cell: nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes.  

5. Function  
   • DNA stores the genetic blueprint for an organism.  
   • RNA plays multiple roles:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA) carries genetic instructions from DNA to the ribosome.  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA) helps form the ribosome’s structure and catalytic core.  
     – Other noncoding RNAs regulate gene expression and RNA processing.  

6. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (the missing 2′-OH makes it less prone to hydrolysis).  
   • RNA is more reactive and generally shorter-lived, which suits its roles in rapid regulation and protein synthesis.  

7. Replication vs. Transcription  
   • DNA replicates itself in a semi-conservative process before cell division.  
   • RNA is synthesized (transcribed) from a DNA template whenever gene products are needed.  

Summary  
DNA is the long-term storage molecule of genetic information, optimized for stability. RNA is more versatile and transient, acting as the intermediary, catalyst, and regulator in gene expression and protein production.
